profile.summary: A small evaluation from the CIViC MCP paper: can a large language model say which CIViC clinical significance labels are supported for a (molecular profile, cancer type, therapy) triplet? GPT-5 was tested alone, with the CIViC MCP server, and in Agent Mode on 100 randomly sampled CIViC triplets. It is relevant to people judging LLM tools for retrieving curated cancer variant evidence; it is one paper's study, not a maintained benchmark.

summary_quotes.text: We selected a controlled classification task: given a CIViC triplet (molecular profile, cancer type, therapy), the LLM must determine which CIViC clinical significance has supporting evidence.
we compared GPT-5’s performance with and without the MCP server on the same set of 100 randomly selected triplets from CIViC Evidence Items. We used a zero-shot prompt at temperature = 1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether an LLM retrieves current CIViC evidence correctly. For each triplet and each candidate clinical significance, the model answers supports, does not support, or no evidence. The authors frame it as a test of retrieval through the MCP server against recall from pretraining or web browsing.

quotes.text: We selected a controlled classification task: given a CIViC triplet (molecular profile, cancer type, therapy), the LLM must determine which CIViC clinical significance has supporting evidence.
These three outcomes served as the class labels for evaluation, allowing us to distinguish between positive evidence, contradictory evidence, and absence of evidence.

Our benchmark shows the server improves the accuracy of clinical significance retrieval while avoiding the far greater latency of GPT-5’s Agent Mode, which navigates the web by simulating human inputs.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: 100 triplets were randomly selected from CIViC Evidence Items; expected answers come from CIViC. The README describes QA_triplet_dataset.csv as holding the triplets and expected answers. The scoring script reads a CIViC evidence extract dated 2_27_26 in its file name. The illustrative example in the paper was chosen separately and is not in the 100.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: GPT-5 is prompted zero-shot at temperature 1. Scoring is at the significance-label level, micro-averaged within each Evidence Type, with the common no-evidence label excluded. Reported metrics are overall accuracy and micro-F1, plus mean response time with a 95% confidence interval; the script uses 10,000 bootstrap resamples. The paper reports GPT-5 with MCP at 0.95 accuracy and 0.98 micro-F1, GPT-5 alone at 0.30 and 0.46, and Agent Mode at 0.83 and 0.91.

quotes.text: we compared GPT-5’s performance with and without the MCP server on the same set of 100 randomly selected triplets from CIViC Evidence Items. We used a zero-shot prompt at temperature = 1

Performance was evaluated at the significance-label level and then summarized at the level of each Evidence Type by micro-averaging across all associated significance labels within that type. We excluded the common “No Evidence” label to avoid inflating global metrics and obscuring errors.
Specifically, GPT-5 + MCP achieved 0.95 overall accuracy and a 0.98 micro-F1, compared with 0.30 overall accuracy and 0.46 micro-F1 for GPT-5 without MCP.
Agent Mode improved markedly over GPT-5 alone, achieving 0.83 overall accuracy and a 0.91 micro-F1, but remained below GPT-5 + MCP while requiring nearly 10-fold longer runtime.
Mean response times were similar for GPT-5 + MCP (43.1 s, 95% CI: 39.7–47.0)
BOOTSTRAP_RESAMPLES = 10000

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository ships the model outputs and the scoring script. Clone it at the pinned commit, install the Python requirements, and run eval_one_shot.py from the eval_QA_experiment folder; it rescores the no-MCP, MCP and Agent Mode outputs and writes summary CSVs. Generating new model answers needs an OpenAI API key and the separate one_shot scripts, which are not covered here.
